overview.main_topic: Passing a list of built-in callbacks to fit(), saving/reloading models, and the start of the custom Callback API
overview.central_idea: Callbacks are passed to fit() as a list; EarlyStopping halts training when a monitored quantity stops improving, and ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True keeps the best model on disk. When no built-in callback fits, you subclass keras.callbacks.Callback and override hook methods such as on_epoch_begin and on_epoch_end.
overview.importance: This is the practical recipe that replaces the wasteful 'train once to find the best epoch, then retrain' strategy used in earlier chapters. It also opens the door to arbitrary custom behaviour inside fit() without writing your own training loop.

summary:
The page opens with **Listing 7.19**, the concrete example promised at the end of p.233. A Python list `callbacks_list` holds two built-in callbacks:

- `keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="accuracy", patience=1)` interrupts training once the monitored accuracy has stopped improving for more than one epoch (the callout clarifies: that is, two epochs).
- `keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(filepath="checkpoint_path.keras", monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True)` saves the model after every epoch, but because of `save_best_only=True` and `monitor="val_loss"` it only overwrites the file when validation loss has improved, so the file always holds the best model seen so far.

The model from `get_mnist_model()` is compiled with Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy, and `metrics=["accuracy"]` - the callouts stress that accuracy must be among the compiled metrics because a callback monitors it. `fit()` is then called with `epochs=10`, `callbacks=callbacks_list` and `validation_data=(val_images, val_labels)`; validation data is required because the checkpoint watches `val_loss`.

The text adds that you can always save a model manually with `model.save("my_checkpoint_path.keras")` and reload a saved model with `keras.models.load_model("checkpoint_path.keras")` - here reloading the file produced by the checkpoint.

**Section 7.3.3, Writing your own callbacks**, begins: if no built-in callback covers the action you need, subclass `keras.callbacks.Callback` and implement any of a set of "transparently named" methods called at points during training. The page lists the first two: `on_epoch_begin(epoch, logs)` (start of every epoch) and `on_epoch_end(epoch, logs)` (end of every epoch). The list of hooks continues on p.235.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Listing 7.19 builds a list of two callbacks (EarlyStopping and ModelCheckpoint), compiles an MNIST model with accuracy as a metric, and passes the list to fit() along with validation data. The callouts explain each argument: callbacks go in a list (any number); EarlyStopping interrupts training when improvement stops, here when accuracy has not improved for more than one epoch (two epochs); ModelCheckpoint saves after every epoch to the given path; monitor='val_loss' plus save_best_only=True means the file is only overwritten when val_loss improves; accuracy must be a compiled metric; and validation_data is needed because validation quantities are monitored.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Training no longer runs blindly for a fixed number of epochs. epochs=10 becomes an upper bound: EarlyStopping can end the run sooner, and whatever happens, ModelCheckpoint leaves the best-by-validation-loss model on disk. Note a small inconsistency on the printed page: the callout says EarlyStopping 'Monitors the model's validation accuracy', but the code says monitor="accuracy", which is the *training* accuracy reported in logs; validation accuracy would be monitor="val_accuracy". As written, the early-stopping criterion is based on training accuracy while the checkpoint criterion is based on validation loss.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This combination is the standard Keras pattern for avoiding wasted epochs and for recovering the best model rather than the last (possibly overfit) one. It reappears in chapter 8 (p.274, p.287) with ModelCheckpoint monitoring val_loss.
paragraphs.technical_idea: patience counts epochs without improvement before stopping. With patience=1, the callback tolerates one non-improving epoch and stops at the end of the second consecutive one. 'Improvement' depends on the mode, which Keras infers from the metric name (max for accuracy, min for loss).

terminology.meaning: Name of the quantity in the logs dict that the callback watches, e.g. 'accuracy', 'val_loss'.
Number of epochs with no improvement tolerated before EarlyStopping interrupts training.
ModelCheckpoint option: only write the file when the monitored quantity improves on its best value so far.
fit() argument giving held-out (inputs, targets); Keras evaluates on it each epoch and adds val_* entries to the logs.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Besides checkpointing during training, you can save a model by hand after training with model.save("my_checkpoint_path.keras"); to reload a saved model, call keras.models.load_model(...) with its path - the example reloads "checkpoint_path.keras".
paragraphs.what_it_means: The .keras file is a full model archive (architecture, weights, and compile/optimizer state), so load_model returns a ready-to-use model without re-running the model-building code. The reload example points at the checkpoint file written by ModelCheckpoint, i.e. the best model from Listing 7.19, not the manually saved one; either filename would work with load_model.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: After a run with save_best_only=True, the in-memory model holds the *last* epoch's weights, which may be worse than the best epoch. Reloading the checkpoint is how you actually get the best model back.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Keras 3 requires the .keras extension for the native format with model.save(); ModelCheckpoint can alternatively save only weights with save_weights_only=True (then the path must end in .weights.h5).

paragraphs.excerpt: If you need to take a specific action during training that isn’t covered
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 7.3.3 starts: when built-in callbacks don't cover what you need, write your own by subclassing keras.callbacks.Callback and implementing any number of 'transparently named' methods that Keras calls at various points during training. The first two shown are on_epoch_begin(epoch, logs), called at the start of every epoch, and on_epoch_end(epoch, logs), called at the end of every epoch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A callback is an observer with a fixed set of hook points. fit() owns the loop and, at each hook point, calls the corresponding method on every callback in the list. You override only the hooks you care about; the base class supplies no-op defaults for the rest.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the extensibility mechanism of fit(): logging, custom schedules, plotting, custom stopping logic and similar behaviour can all be injected without abandoning the built-in loop. The full list of hooks and the logs argument continue on p.235, followed by Listing 7.20.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Inside a callback, self.model gives access to the model being trained (Keras sets it before training starts), so a hook can read or change weights, read the optimizer, or set self.model.stop_training = True.

terminology.meaning: Base class for all callbacks; subclass it and override hook methods.
Hooks invoked at the start/end of every epoch with the epoch index and a logs dict.

connections: p.235: the remaining hooks (on_batch_*, on_train_*) and the meaning of logs
p.232: a callback is an object called by the model at various points during training

concepts.name: Keras callback
concepts.definition: An object (subclass of keras.callbacks.Callback) passed to fit() in a list and invoked by the training loop at defined points (epoch/batch/training start and end).
concepts.intuition: Sensors and autopilot attached to fit(): they observe the run and can act on it.
concepts.technical: fit() iterates over the callbacks list and calls hook methods with an index and a logs dict of current metrics. Callbacks can access self.model.
concepts.significance: Lets you customize training behaviour without writing a custom loop.
concepts.misconception: Callbacks are not part of the model; they belong to a particular fit() call and are not saved with the model.

concepts.name: EarlyStopping callback
concepts.definition: Built-in callback that interrupts training when a monitored metric has stopped improving for more than `patience` epochs.
concepts.intuition: Stop paying for epochs that no longer help.
concepts.technical: Tracks the best value of `monitor`; increments a wait counter on each non-improving epoch; when the counter exceeds patience it sets model.stop_training = True. Optional restore_best_weights (not on this page) reloads the best weights.
concepts.significance: Turns epochs into an upper bound and saves compute; complements checkpointing.
concepts.example: EarlyStopping(monitor="accuracy", patience=1) stops after two consecutive epochs without accuracy improvement.
concepts.misconception: monitor="accuracy" is training accuracy, not validation accuracy; for generalization-based stopping you would usually monitor a val_* quantity.

concepts.name: ModelCheckpoint callback
concepts.definition: Built-in callback that saves the model (or weights) to disk at the end of epochs.
concepts.intuition: A save point in a video game, kept only when you beat your best score.
concepts.technical: With save_best_only=True, compares the monitored quantity to its best value so far and writes filepath only on improvement.
concepts.significance: Guarantees you keep the best model even if training continues into overfitting.
concepts.misconception: After training, the model object in memory is the last epoch's model, not the checkpointed best one; you must reload the file.

concepts.name: Saving and loading models
concepts.definition: model.save(path) writes a full .keras archive; keras.models.load_model(path) restores it.
concepts.intuition: Freeze-drying the trained model so you can revive it later exactly as it was.
concepts.technical: The .keras format stores architecture config, weights and optimizer/compile state.
concepts.significance: Needed to reuse the best checkpoint or deploy a trained model.
concepts.misconception: Models with custom layers/classes need those classes available (e.g. via custom_objects) when loading - beyond this page.

concepts.name: Custom callback
concepts.definition: A user subclass of keras.callbacks.Callback that overrides hook methods like on_epoch_begin/on_epoch_end.
concepts.intuition: Writing your own sensor plugin for fit().
concepts.technical: Override any subset of hooks; each receives an index (epoch or batch) and a logs dict.
concepts.significance: Covers actions no built-in callback provides.
concepts.example: Listing 7.20 on p.235 records per-batch losses and plots them.
concepts.misconception: You do not need to implement all hooks; unimplemented ones default to doing nothing.

code.title: Using the callbacks argument in the fit() method
code.original_code:
callbacks_list = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
        monitor="accuracy",
        patience=1,
    ),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(
        filepath="checkpoint_path.keras",
        monitor="val_loss",
        save_best_only=True,
    ),
]
model = get_mnist_model()
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    train_images,
    train_labels,
    epochs=10,
    callbacks=callbacks_list,
    validation_data=(val_images, val_labels),
)
code.what_it_does: Trains the MNIST model for at most 10 epochs, stopping early if training accuracy stalls for two epochs, and keeps the model with the lowest validation loss in checkpoint_path.keras.

line_explanations.explanation: Callbacks are collected in a plain Python list; fit() accepts any number.

EarlyStopping watching 'accuracy' with patience=1: stop when accuracy has failed to improve for more than one epoch. Callout says 'validation accuracy', but the key is training accuracy ('val_accuracy' would be validation).
ModelCheckpoint: evaluated after every epoch; writes to checkpoint_path.keras only when val_loss beats its best value (save_best_only=True).
Build and compile the model; metrics=["accuracy"] is required so that 'accuracy' appears in the logs EarlyStopping reads.
fit() with the callbacks list; validation_data makes Keras compute val_loss/val_accuracy at the end of each epoch, which ModelCheckpoint needs.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: train_images/train_labels and val_images/val_labels (MNIST splits prepared earlier in section 7.3). Outputs: a trained model in memory (last epoch's weights), a History object (returned but not stored here), and checkpoint_path.keras on disk with the best model by val_loss.
code.algorithm: For each epoch up to 10: train on all batches; evaluate on validation data; call on_epoch_end on each callback -> ModelCheckpoint compares val_loss to best and maybe saves; EarlyStopping compares accuracy to best, updates its wait counter, maybe sets stop_training.
code.theory_link: Implements the early-stopping regularization strategy from p.185: find the boundary between underfitting and overfitting without a second training run.

parameters.name: monitor
parameters.role: Logs key watched by each callback ('accuracy', 'val_loss').

parameters.name: patience
parameters.role: Epochs without improvement tolerated before stopping (1 here -> stops after 2 bad epochs).

parameters.name: filepath
parameters.role: Destination of the saved model; .keras extension for the full-model format.

parameters.name: save_best_only
parameters.role: Only overwrite the file on improvement of monitor.

pitfalls: Monitoring a metric that wasn't compiled (or a val_* metric without validation_data) makes the callback warn and do nothing useful.
monitor="accuracy" is training accuracy; it tends to keep rising even while the model overfits, so it is a weak early-stopping signal.
The model in memory after fit() is the last epoch's, not the best checkpoint - reload the file.
patience=1 is very aggressive; noisy metrics can trigger a premature stop.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written variant (not in the book): stop on validation accuracy
# and restore the best weights automatically
callbacks_list = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_accuracy", patience=2,
                                  restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint("checkpoint_path.keras",
                                    monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True),
]
history = model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=10,
                    callbacks=callbacks_list,
                    validation_data=(val_images, val_labels))
best = keras.models.load_model("checkpoint_path.keras")

deeper.title: Tracing patience=1 epoch by epoch
deeper.body:
Suppose training accuracy per epoch is 0.90, 0.94, 0.95, 0.95, 0.949.

1. Epoch 0: best = 0.90, wait = 0.
2. Epoch 1: 0.94 > best -> best = 0.94, wait = 0.
3. Epoch 2: 0.95 -> best = 0.95, wait = 0.
4. Epoch 3: 0.95 is not an improvement -> wait = 1 (equal to patience, keep going).
5. Epoch 4: 0.949 -> wait = 2 > patience -> stop.

So with patience=1 training stops after **two** consecutive non-improving epochs, exactly the callout's "more than one epoch (that is, two epochs)". Meanwhile ModelCheckpoint, independently, saved the file at every epoch where val_loss reached a new minimum. (Illustrative numbers; Keras also supports a min_delta threshold.)

deeper.title: Why two different monitored quantities?
deeper.body: In Listing 7.19 the two callbacks watch different signals: EarlyStopping watches training `accuracy`, ModelCheckpoint watches `val_loss`. This is legal - each callback reads its own key from the same logs dict - but it is worth noticing. Training accuracy usually keeps improving while overfitting sets in, so stopping on it will tend to let training run longer than a validation-based criterion would; the checkpoint still protects you by keeping the best-val_loss model. In practice (and as p.233 suggests, stopping "when the validation loss is no longer improving"), people commonly monitor a validation quantity for both. The callout's phrase 'validation accuracy' suggests the authors may have intended `val_accuracy`.

deeper.title: Paper airplane to drone, concretely
deeper.body: p.232 compares plain fit() to a paper airplane and fit() with callbacks to a drone. In this listing, EarlyStopping is the drone's 'land when you stop climbing' rule and ModelCheckpoint is its black-box recorder that keeps the best footage. Custom callbacks (7.3.3) let you program new rules into the drone.

flowchart TD
 A[epoch e starts] --> B[on_epoch_begin on each callback]
 B --> C[train on all batches]

 D --> E[on_epoch_end with logs]

 K -- yes --> A
 K -- no --> J

misconceptions.claim: monitor="accuracy" makes EarlyStopping watch validation accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: "accuracy" is the training metric; validation accuracy is "val_accuracy" and requires validation_data. The listing's callout describes it as validation accuracy, which does not match the code.

misconceptions.claim: After fit() with ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True), the model variable holds the best model.
misconceptions.correction: It holds the weights from the last completed epoch. The best model is in the file; reload it with keras.models.load_model.

misconceptions.claim: patience=1 stops training at the first epoch without improvement.
misconceptions.correction: It tolerates one non-improving epoch and stops after more than one, i.e. after two consecutive non-improving epochs.

misconceptions.claim: To customize anything during training you must write your own training loop.
misconceptions.correction: Subclassing keras.callbacks.Callback lets you hook into fit() at epoch/batch/train boundaries without leaving the built-in loop.

takeaways: Pass callbacks to fit() as a list via the callbacks argument; any number is allowed.
EarlyStopping(monitor, patience) stops training once the monitored quantity fails to improve for more than `patience` epochs.
ModelCheckpoint(filepath, monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True) keeps the best model seen during training on disk.
Monitored metrics must be compiled, and val_* quantities require validation_data.
Save manually with model.save("....keras") and reload with keras.models.load_model().
Custom callbacks subclass keras.callbacks.Callback and override hooks like on_epoch_begin and on_epoch_end.

questions.question: In Listing 7.19, why is validation_data passed to fit()?
options: Because EarlyStopping always requires validation data
Because ModelCheckpoint monitors val_loss, which is only computed when validation data is provided
Because save_best_only=True only works with MNIST
Because the Adam optimizer needs a validation set
questions.answer: Because ModelCheckpoint monitors val_loss, which is only computed when validation data is provided
questions.explanation: val_* entries appear in logs only if fit() evaluates on validation data. EarlyStopping here monitors training accuracy, so it alone would not need it; the other options are unrelated to the optimizer or dataset.

questions.question: With EarlyStopping(monitor="accuracy", patience=1), after how many consecutive non-improving epochs does training stop?
questions.explanation: The callout says training is interrupted when accuracy has stopped improving for more than one epoch, that is, two epochs.

questions.question: What exactly do monitor="val_loss" and save_best_only=True together guarantee about checkpoint_path.keras?
questions.answer: The file is only overwritten when validation loss improves on its best value so far, so at the end it contains the model with the lowest val_loss seen during training.
questions.explanation: This is the callout's 'you won't overwrite the model file unless val_loss has improved, which allows you to keep the best model seen during training.'

questions.question: Which key would make EarlyStopping watch validation accuracy rather than training accuracy?
questions.explanation: Keras prefixes validation metrics with val_. "accuracy" (used in the listing) is the training metric; the other two names are not keys Keras produces.

questions.question: Why does the listing need metrics=["accuracy"] in compile()?
questions.answer: Because EarlyStopping monitors 'accuracy'; a callback can only monitor quantities that appear in the logs, and accuracy appears only if it is a compiled metric.
questions.explanation: The callout: 'You monitor accuracy, so it should be part of the model's metrics.'

questions.question: How do you implement a callback for an action no built-in callback covers, and which method runs at the end of every epoch?
questions.answer: Subclass keras.callbacks.Callback and override hook methods; on_epoch_end(epoch, logs) runs at the end of every epoch.
questions.explanation: Section 7.3.3 states callbacks are implemented by subclassing keras.callbacks.Callback and lists on_epoch_begin/on_epoch_end.

questions.question: After training with Listing 7.19, you call model.evaluate() on the test set immediately. Is that evaluating the best model? What would you do instead?
questions.answer: No - the in-memory model has the last epoch's weights. Reload the best model with keras.models.load_model("checkpoint_path.keras") and evaluate that.
questions.explanation: ModelCheckpoint saves to disk but does not change the in-memory model; the page shows load_model for exactly this purpose.
